anchor.quote: Write and design content that matches how users read.

not_rules.note: Page-level introduction to the specific writing and design guidance, not an additional finding for every failure below.

anchor.prefix: nt that matches how users read.
anchor.quote: Use short sentences and simple structure.

not_rules.note: The two components are covered by the specific sentence-length and section-heading checks.

anchor.quote: To create usable content, take into account how people read and what makes content easy to read.

not_rules.note: G-5: asks writers to consider reading behaviour; it does not identify a separate textual violation.

anchor.quote: You can increase usability with:

not_rules.note: Introduces factors affecting usability, not a separate check for each listed factor.

anchor.quote: You must understand the needs of all users of your service and create content they can access to meet the Digital Service Standard:

not_rules.note: G-5: states a user-research and service-compliance duty rather than a determinate additional property of the text. The concrete accessibility instructions are considered separately.

anchor.quote: To help people understand the type of content, use a clear structure.

not_rules.note: G-4: absorbed into the more specific instruction to organise content using section headings.

anchor.quote: Make sure users can navigate through all content in the intended order, regardless of the technology they're using.

not_rules.note: Concerns navigation and technology-dependent access order, rather than a rule about the words themselves.

anchor.quote: Use the same navigation elements across the service.

not_rules.note: Requires consistency of service navigation elements; it does not specifically prescribe navigation wording.

anchor.quote: Don’t rely on colour alone to structure pages.

not_rules.note: Concerns visual page presentation and colour-dependent structure.

anchor.quote: Write in plain language.

anchor.quote: Rhythm changes can help or hinder reading

not_rules.note: G-1: the candidate heading groups the discussions of sentence length, paragraphs, line breaks and variations in rhythm. It does not itself instruct a check.

anchor.quote: Help people build reading rhythm with:

anchor.quote: For example, you can use a change of rhythm for emphasis: to make a point or draw the reader's attention to a certain word.

not_rules.note: G-3: recorded as a permitted use under the comprehension rule, not an independent requirement to vary rhythm.

anchor.quote: You can vary rhythm using:

not_rules.note: G-3: introduces possible techniques, not requirements to use them or prohibitions on them.

anchor.quote: Use capital letters appropriately to help people understand written English.

not_rules.note: G-5: a general exhortation to follow appropriate capitalisation, with no specific casing convention to test. Do not turn the preceding demonstration into an unstated blanket ban on capitals.

rules.quote: Structure the page to make the most useful content stand out.
rules.specification: The page does not define how to identify the most useful content or how much prominence it needs. These require an understanding of user needs and the page's presentation.
rules.violation_condition: The information most useful to the page's users is buried or obscured by the page structure rather than made prominent.
when: Applies to the discussion of structuring content for reading on screens.
rules.why: This is a distinct instruction about information prominence, not a general prohibition on particular layouts.

rules.quote: For this reason, present information in an accepted pattern such as:
rules.specification: The page illustrates accepted patterns with an address block and underlined hyperlinks. It supplies neither an exhaustive inventory of patterns nor exact address-format requirements; do not infer those requirements.
rules.violation_condition: Information that users scan for is presented in an unfamiliar arrangement rather than a recognisable conventional pattern.
when: Applies to information users seek by scanning, such as an address or a link.
The listed patterns are examples, not a statement that every other presentation is wrong.
rules.why: G-2: the examples illustrate one conventional-presentation check, not separate universal requirements for every formatting detail.

rules.specification: Interpret clarity as communicating the page's subject or purpose. The page gives no title-length limit or prescribed wording.
rules.violation_condition: A page title is too vague or unclear to communicate the page's subject or purpose.
rules.why: Title clarity and alignment with the first heading can fail independently, so they are separate checks.

rules.quote: This is the first thing a screen reader user will hear and should align with the first heading on the page.
rules.specification: ‘This’ refers to the page title. Interpret alignment as consistency of subject and purpose, not a requirement for identical wording.
rules.violation_condition: The page title and the first heading communicate inconsistent subjects or purposes.
rules.why: G-4: retain the body sentence that states the title–heading relationship rather than treating it as another title-clarity instruction.

covers.quote: To help people understand the type of content, use a clear structure.

rules.quote: Organise content with a clear structure using section headings.
rules.violation_condition: Content has distinct sections but lacks section headings that expose its organisation.
when: Applies to content organised into sections.
rules.why: G-1 and G-4: use the specific section-heading instruction rather than also flagging the broad clear-structure summaries.

rules.quote: Describe the topics or the following section in the heading.
rules.violation_condition: A heading does not identify the topic or content of the section that follows it.
rules.why: A missing section heading and an existing but uninformative heading are different findings.

rules.quote: Don’t rely on sensory characteristics such as shape, size, visual location, orientation or sound to explain things.
rules.violation_condition: An explanation depends on sensory characteristics to identify a referent or communicate an action, without sufficient non-sensory information.
when: Assess whether the surrounding explanation supplies enough information without relying on the sensory characteristic.
rules.why: This constrains the wording of explanations, unlike the neighbouring instructions about navigation implementation and page colour.

rules.quote: Level AAA requires a lower secondary education reading level, after removal of proper names and titles (year 7 or between 12 and 14 years old).
rules.specification: The target is lower secondary education, described as year 7 or ages 12–14. The page does not specify a reading-level assessment method.
rules.violation_condition: Content required to meet Level AAA exceeds a lower secondary education reading level after proper names and titles are removed.
when: Applies when WCAG Level AAA conformance is required.
Remove proper names and titles before assessing the reading level.
rules.why: G-2: the conformance level and removal of names and titles are conditions on one reading-level check.

rules.quote: Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on.
rules.specification: What counts as unusual depends on the intended readers. The page supplies no vocabulary list or fixed test, and does not prescribe where explanations must appear.
rules.violation_condition: An unusual word, phrase or idiom appears without an explanation that makes it understandable to the intended readers.
when: An unusual expression is permitted when it is explained.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: avoidance and explanation are alternative ways to satisfy one check, not two rules.

rules.quote: Expand all acronyms on their first use.
rules.violation_condition: An acronym's first occurrence lacks its expansion.
when: Check the first use of each acronym.
The page states no exception for familiar acronyms.
rules.why: First-use expansion is independently testable and is not merely another unusual-word finding.

rules.violation_condition: A sentence contains a double negative.
rules.why: Keep the specific double-negative check rather than duplicating it under a general plain-language rule.

rules.quote: For most readers, aim for an average sentence length of 15 words per sentence.
rules.specification: Operationalise the aim as flagging a mean above 15 words, without flagging lower means. This upper-target interpretation is not an explicit hard limit in the manual.
rules.violation_condition: Content for most readers has a document-wide average sentence length above the 15-word target.
when: Applies to content intended for most readers.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the short-sentence summaries; E-4 requires the operational interpretation of ‘aim for’ to be explicit.

rules.quote: Long sentences should have no more than 25 words.
rules.violation_condition: An individual sentence contains more than 25 words.
rules.why: An individual sentence can exceed 25 words even when the document meets the average target, so these are separate checks.

covers.quote: For example, you can use a change of rhythm for emphasis: to make a point or draw the reader's attention to a certain word.

rules.specification: The page gives no measurable test for whether a rhythm change supports comprehension. Do not infer a prohibition on headings, lists, punctuation, parenthetical information, capitals or italics merely because they can interrupt rhythm.
rules.violation_condition: A variation in reading rhythm disrupts understanding rather than supporting comprehension.
when: Applies to variations in reading rhythm.
Changes of rhythm for emphasis are permitted when they support comprehension.
Headings, lists, punctuation and parenthetical information are possible means of varying rhythm, not inherently violations.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: keep one comprehension check with permitted uses, rather than turning every listed interruption into a prohibition.
